extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars interested in philosophy, social attitudes, psychology, and cultural studies
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and classifying the concept of misanthropy: its definitions, types, causes, forms of life, arguments for and against, empirical correlates, and cultural expressions. Useful for someone writing about or studying misanthropy in philosophy, social science, or literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of misanthropy
rubrics_metrics.description: Misanthropy is the general hatred, dislike, or distrust of the human species, human behavior, or human nature; in contemporary philosophy it is usually understood as a negative evaluation of humanity as a whole based on humanity's vices and flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasises that misanthropy can have both emotional and cognitive components (not just blind rejection), and that hatred is only one possible form of expression. It notes etymology (Greek μῖσος 'hatred' + ἄνθρωπος 'human').

rubrics_metrics.name: Ubiquity/scope requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: One central aspect of misanthropy is that the negative attitude is not local but ubiquitous — directed at humanity as a whole rather than just particular individuals or groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes misanthropy from other discriminatory attitudes (misogyny, racism, etc.). The article notes that 'horizon' matters: a person who loathes every villager could be a misanthrope relative to that horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kantian positive vs negative misanthropy
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant's distinction: positive misanthropes are active enemies who wish harm on humanity; negative misanthropes are peaceful anthropophobes who withdraw from society and may wish others well despite their negative appraisal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this split to evaluate whether misanthropy is destructive/active or isolating/passive; Kant links negative misanthropy with moral disappointment from bad experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-inclusive vs self-aggrandizing misanthropy
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes whether the negative assessment includes the self (self-inclusive) or excludes the self and views oneself as superior (self-aggrandizing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-aggrandizing variants often involve hypocrisy and inflated ego; the distinction matters for evaluating consistency and ethical implications of the misanthropic stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Babbitt: naked intellect vs tender misanthropy
rubrics_metrics.description: Babbitt's categorization: 'misanthropes of the naked intellect' view humanity as hopeless with no exceptions, while 'tender misanthropes' exclude a few idealized people from their negative evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to assess how absolutist or exception-permitting a misanthropic claim is; Rousseau cited as tender misanthrope, Swift as emblematic of the naked-intellect type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude basis taxonomy (Svoboda): dislike, hate, contempt, judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Svoboda distinguishes misanthropy grounded in dislike, hate, contempt, or judgment; only judgment-based misanthropy is presented as a serious philosophical position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this to judge whether a misanthropic claim is emotional (dislike/hate), evaluative but biased (contempt), or reasoned/theoretical (judgment). Svoboda argues contempt is biased and dislike/hate resist objective assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of misanthropic life (destructive, fugitive, activist, quietist, humor-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misanthropy can express in practical life as destructive (aiming to harm humanity), fugitive (seeking isolation), activist (trying to improve humanity via meliorism), quietist (resigned avoidance), or humor-based (mockery and ridicule of human absurdity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These archetypes identify dominant emotions and practical consequences; the article warns archetypes are simplified but useful. The humor-based approach uses mockery as mirror and palliative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human flaws as basis (moral, intellectual, aesthetic, spiritual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misanthropy's negative evaluation is grounded in perceived human flaws which are often categorized as moral flaws, intellectual flaws, aesthetic flaws, and spiritual flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats moral flaws as most serious but documents each category with examples (e.g., cruelty, dogmatism, ugliness) and notes debates about entrenched vs non-essential flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral flaws (list and weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral flaws cited include cruelty, selfishness, injustice, greed, indifference to suffering, cowardice, moral laziness, ingratitude, and complicity in large harms (genocide, factory farming, pollution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral flaws are often given special importance in arguments for misanthropy because of human moral responsibility and the scale of harm; examples and historical atrocities are used as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual flaws (list and mechanisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual flaws include dogmatism, arrogance, wishful thinking, stupidity, gullibility, and cognitive biases (confirmation bias, self-serving bias, hindsight bias, anchoring bias), as well as self-deceit and wilful ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These flaws are cited as both direct harms and enablers of moral failings (they obscure recognition and correction of vice). Some traditions consider ignorance the root of evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic flaws (scope and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic flaws relate to ugliness and insensitivity to beauty, including revulsion at bodily functions, pollution-caused ugliness, and loss of aesthetic sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While usually given less weight than moral/intellectual flaws, aesthetic considerations sometimes contribute to misanthropic evaluations of humanity and its activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological causes of misanthropy
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual psychological factors include disappointments, disillusionments, loss of trust following negative experiences (especially for initially optimistic people), revulsion toward the human body/sexuality, and moral superiority feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/philosophical examples (Plato, Hobbes, Schopenhauer) are used to illustrate how personal adversity can foster misanthropy; the article suggests these factors increase likelihood but may not fully explain development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and political causes (inequality, regime type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broader social circumstances that foster misanthropy include socio-economic inequality (undermining trust), authoritarian regimes (repression increasing misanthropy), whereas democracy may reduce it by allowing freedom and optimism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies are cited linking low socioeconomic status, minority status, recent negative events, and lower church attendance to higher misanthropy; political attitudes such as support for authoritarian policies also correlate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical measurement indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical studies often operationalize misanthropy using survey questions about trust in other people (whether others would be fair and helpful) and correlate responses with demographic and attitudinal variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trust-related questions and statistical correlates (SES, race/ethnicity, church attendance, political views) when measuring misanthropy in social research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments for misanthropy (basis and emphases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments for misanthropy focus on human-caused harms (wars, genocides, factory farming, environmental destruction), moral responsibility (humans can understand consequences but choose otherwise), ordinary everyday vices, and long-term ecological catastrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents either emphasize extreme cases or ordinary complicity; ecological and extinction-based arguments (anti-natalism, human extinction movements) also derive from misanthropic premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main criticisms of misanthropy
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms include: extreme cases do not justify condemning humanity at large; humans also have virtues and achievements; the negative evaluation may be better aimed at social forces (capitalism, patriarchy, etc.); misanthropy has social and personal costs (violence, misery, friendlessness); it can be inconsistent or self-contradictory; and may be pathological or unnatural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These objections are used to challenge both the accuracy and desirability of misanthropic positions, and to distinguish between legitimate critique of institutions versus blanket condemnation of humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to philosophical pessimism
rubrics_metrics.description: Misanthropy is closely related but not identical to philosophical pessimism; pessimism holds life/world is bad or meaningless, and may accompany misanthropy when humans are also judged blameworthy, but the two views can be held separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction helps clarify whether the negative evaluation targets human agency/morality specifically (misanthropy) or a more general metaphysical/valuation of existence (pessimism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misanthropy and antinatalism/human extinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'misanthropic argument' for antinatalism holds that because humans cause extensive harm, there is a moral duty to abstain from procreation; related social movements (Voluntary Human Extinction Movement, Church of Euthanasia) explicitly endorse anti-natalist or extinctionist aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies a specific ethical/political consequence of misanthropic thought and links misanthropy to debates about procreation and the desirability of humanity's future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human exceptionalism and deep ecology relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Human exceptionalism (claiming unique importance of humans) is often opposed by misanthropic or deep-ecology perspectives that criticize privileging human well-being over other species; deep ecology critics sometimes accuse the movement of misanthropy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this dimension to evaluate whether a position rejects or defends human centrality and to locate misanthropy within environmental ethics debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature and popular-culture manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: Misanthropy appears in literature and popular culture (examples: Timon of Athens, The Misanthrope, Gulliver's Travels, Ebenezer Scrooge, the Joker) as character types and themes that portray negative appraisals of humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples function as illustrative cases for understanding the forms, consequences, and expressions of misanthropy and can be used as touchstones when analyzing cultural representations.
